analysis.one_liner: Lets the Treasury Secretary waive penalties for failing to disclose tax-avoidance transactions.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond its referral on June 12, 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, taxpayers who use transactions the IRS has flagged as having "potential for tax avoidance or evasion" must disclose them, and the penalty for not doing so can only be rescinded in narrow circumstances. This bill would have let the Treasury Secretary waive or reduce that penalty for any taxpayer who had "reasonable cause" and acted in good faith, and would have barred courts from reviewing those waiver decisions. It was introduced by Rep. Jerry Moran in June 2008, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received any further action before the Congress ended [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who fail to disclose transactions the IRS considers potentially abusive — including users of listed tax-avoidance transactions — would gain a new path to have their penalties wiped out or reduced by the Treasury Secretary, with no possibility of court review of that decision. Tax practitioners and promoters of such transactions also benefit from a softer disclosure-enforcement regime [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds a waiver whenever the taxpayer shows reasonable cause and acted in good faith, on top of the existing 'promote compliance' exception [S2][S3].
Moves rescission and waiver authority from the IRS Commissioner to the Treasury Secretary, giving the political head of the Treasury Department discretion over these penalties [S2][S3].
Requires the Secretary to document in writing the facts, reasons, and dollar amount of any penalty waived [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The disclosure requirement exists so the IRS can identify and track tax-avoidance schemes; making the penalty easier to waive weakens that enforcement tool, and the cost falls on general taxpayers if undisclosed avoidance transactions go undetected and unpenalized [S2].

drawbacks.text: Weakening the disclosure penalty makes it easier for taxpayers to hide transactions the IRS has identified as having potential for tax avoidance or evasion, since a waiver for 'reasonable cause' becomes broadly available [S2].
The bill explicitly bars any judicial review of the Secretary's waiver decisions, so the decision to erase a penalty would be unreviewable in court [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a legitimate complaint buried in this bill: the disclosure penalty at issue was known for hitting taxpayers with large fines over paperwork failures even when they owed little or no extra tax. But the remedy proposed here goes further in the other direction — it hands the penalty-waiver decision to the political Treasury Secretary with a loose 'reasonable cause' standard and strips courts of any review, which undermines the disclosure system the IRS relies on to detect tax shelters. The bill was also never developed: it received no hearing or markups before dying in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry Moran of Kansas introduced the bill on June 12, 2008, with Reps. Donnelly and Platts joining as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which was the only action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill attracted two cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The stricter disclosure-penalty regime stayed on the books, which serves IRS enforcement of tax-shelter disclosure. Taxpayers who used undisclosed avoidance transactions remain exposed to the full penalties that this bill would have let the Treasury waive.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had mixed-party support (one Republican sponsor, one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor), but it never reached a vote, so no party positions were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Users of reportable tax-avoidance transactions and their advisors
industries.note: The bill would have given them a path to erase penalties for failing to disclose transactions the IRS flags as potentially abusive, but it died, so the penalties remain. Its interest ran against the public's interest in detectable tax shelters.

The bill would have shifted waiver power from the IRS Commissioner to the Treasury Secretary, taking away some of the IRS's control over these penalties while leaving the disclosure regime itself intact.
